CommitmentCOP31 watchLatest development 29 October 2026

The Antalya Compact for Energy Efficient Buildings opens for endorsement

COP31 Presidency · Global (UN climate process)

Ahead of the conference, the COP31 Presidency launched the Antalya Compact for Energy Efficient Buildings, which aims for a 25% cut in the operational energy intensity of buildings worldwide by 2035, compared with 2020. Its actions include stronger energy codes, faster renovation and the electrification of heating and cooling. It covers buildings and energy as a whole, not heat alone; it bears on heat because cooler, more efficient buildings ease the indoor heat people live and work in, and the cost of cooling them.

Heat link: Common Shade's reading The checked text concerns the energy use of buildings; the link to cooling and indoor heat is Common Shade's reading.

Only 35% of countries report health early warning systems for heat-related illness

International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies · Global

IFRC's call to action for COP31 notes that only 35% of countries have reported having health early warning systems for heat-related illness. It asks for investment in multi-sector local action for cities and communities to reduce heat risk, from heat action plans and early warning to shock-responsive social protection and nature-based solutions.

What to watchA finding and an ask, not a commitment: watch whether COP31 outcomes fund heat early warning that reaches health services and communities.

FindingCOP31 watchLatest development September 2026

98% of surveyed maternity and newborn clinicians say they have cared for a pregnant woman they believe heat harmed

Wellcome (commissioned the survey) · Australia, Brazil, India, the UK and Zimbabwe

A survey commissioned by Wellcome asked 1,000 practising clinicians in pregnancy, childbirth, postnatal and newborn care, 250 of them midwives, in Australia, Brazil, India, the UK and Zimbabwe (fieldwork by Censuswide, September 2026). Across the five countries, 98% said they had cared for a pregnant woman, and 99% for a baby, whose health they believed extreme heat had harmed; 73% reported more heat-related complications in pregnant women over the past five years and 76% in foetal or newborn health, and 92% want more training and resources. As reported by Down To Earth, among the 200 respondents in India, 62% reported more complications in pregnant women and 66% in foetal or newborn health, and 26% had seen pregnancy complications that needed extra monitoring or treatment. The findings were presented on 13 November on the sidelines of COP31 in Antalya, where a UN Climate Change official said that about 1% of formal climate finance goes to health. These are clinicians' reports of what they believe they have seen, not measured outcomes. What clinicians in India can already use: on 6 May 2026 the health ministry and UNFPA India published guidance on heat and pregnancy for healthcare providers and community health workers, with a heat-risk checklist, preparedness for health facilities including functional referral systems, and counselling that covers breastfeeding.

What to watchA finding, not a commitment: watch whether the guidance clinicians already have reaches antenatal clinics and community health workers before the hot season, and whether national heat plans and health budgets fund it.

CommitmentLatest development August 2026

India adds heatwaves to its notified natural calamities

Government of India · India

In August 2026 India added heatwaves to its notified natural calamities, so national and state disaster response funds can pay for heatwave relief. Before, states could spend only up to 10% of their response fund on locally declared disasters such as heat. Heat mitigation projects are funded separately, from disaster mitigation funds.

FindingLatest development May 2026

April's pre-monsoon heatwave was made three times more likely

World Weather Attribution · India and South Asia

Fifteen days of heat in late April 2026 pushed India's electricity demand to a record and brought farm drought to more than a million square kilometres. Scientists found climate change made it three times more likely, and that April heat like this now returns about every five years.

What to watchA finding, not a commitment: watch whether plans are sized to heat that now returns about every five years.

Adaptation finance covers a fraction of what is needed

UN Environment Programme · Developing countries

UNEP's Adaptation Gap Report 2026 estimates that developing countries need about US$305 billion a year for adaptation by 2035. International public adaptation finance to developing countries was about US$28 to 32 billion in 2024. Even if the COP30 aim of tripling it is met, it would cover only about 20 to 29% of needs. The report covers adaptation as a whole, not heat alone; it bears on heat because heat plans draw on the same adaptation money.

Heat link: Common Shade's reading The figures are for adaptation finance as a whole; no share for heat is given, and none is implied here.

What to watchA finding, not a commitment: watch whether COP31's finance outcomes reach heat plans, and whether heat is named in them.
